records.name: Erzincan
records.current_summary: Every province in Türkiye sits under the same intensifying national framework. A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package (October 2025) would criminalise LGBT conduct and advocacy — up to 3 years for behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and 4 years for same-sex ceremonies — and would raise gender-affirming-care eligibility from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate, exposing providers to fines and up to 7 years and patients to up to 3 years; 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. The Kaos GL 2025 human-rights report ('A Major Siege', published February 2026) finds hostility became explicit state policy in 2025 — presidency-centred, implemented through the family ministry — documenting 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment cases (up from 51) and 313 liberty violations (about 2.5-fold), counted from media coverage because the state keeps no hate-crime statistics.  No province-specific ordinance, incident series or court decision concerning trans visitors in Erzincan was documented in this research pass; the national framework above is the whole documented picture for Erzincan. The absence of recorded provincial enforcement is not evidence of local tolerance, and equally not evidence of a local ban.

sources.claim: Human Rights news release (29 October 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package omnibus draft law would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years), sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility conditions) and allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care; the government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals"; the package also carries unrelated measures such as longer child sentences and online-content removal.

National-framework page for the law Erzincan province (like every Turkish province) stands under; no Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident or court decision was locatable in this pass, so this framework is the documented picture. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery is legal since 1988, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited; but same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption receive no legal recognition, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military. Since 2015 the authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia; in early 2026 the government was reported to be considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

ILGA-Europe press release (7 December 2020) urging Turkish courts to acquit 19 human rights defenders prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University (METU) in Ankara in May 2019. It documents that even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution in Turkey and calls on the state to uphold its domestic and international commitments and dismiss all charges. It reflects the national freedom-of-assembly climate and legal exposure of LGBT advocacy that a visitor in Erzincan province would be judged against under the same national framework.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 Oct 2025): a leaked omnibus draft (the '11th Judicial Package') would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years), criminalise same-sex ceremonies (up to 4 years), raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment; 15 LGBT groups and the national medical association object.

Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Hatay included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since October 2018 governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally; Istanbul pride was banned repeatedly (police dispersed 2015 and 2016 parades with water cannon and tear gas; on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned). The page records a February 2026 press report that the government was considering a law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a sentence of one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

records.name: Isparta
records.current_summary: A trans visitor in Isparta is subject to the same nationwide developments as anywhere else in the country. An October 2025 leaked omnibus draft would amend the penal code to imprison acts deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality (up to three years; up to four for same-sex ceremonies), restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people 25 and over under infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and expose doctors to up to seven years in prison; national monitoring reports that 2025 hostility became explicit state policy — family-year directives from the head of state, a rights organisation closed, broadcast and arts-event censorship, three hate-motivated killings, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and a 2.5-fold rise in detentions.  No statute, incident or court case specific to Isparta appears in the surviving sources for this record: the documents behind it are national-level and carry no provincial breakdown. The absence of province-specific documentation is not evidence of local tolerance — the nationwide framework and its 2025-26 escalation reach this province as any other.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports a leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's 2025 review finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy — "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The report documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings (trans people the most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), roughly 313 total violations overall — about 2.5 times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.
